evidence.quote: A compiler translates a source program into an equivalent target representation while preserving defined observable behavior. The target may be machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language. A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler, not a fundamentally separate noncompiler technology. A compiler preserves language semantics, not the programmer’s unstated intention.

An interpreter executes a program representation; it need not work one source line at a time. Systems can compile to bytecode and then interpret or JIT-compile it. AOT compilation happens before execution; JIT compilation happens during execution and may use runtime profiles. Neither is universally faster; startup cost, optimization and workload matter.

questions.stem: What is the difference between lexical analysis and syntax analysis?
questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Lexical analysis groups characters into tokens; syntax analysis groups tokens into structures.
answer.explanation: COMP41 separates character-to-token classification from token-to-expression or statement structure. The scanner recognizes lexemes such as identifiers and operators and emits an ordered token stream. The parser checks how those tokens form grammatical constructs and can build a parse tree or AST; legal tokens can still appear in an illegal syntactic arrangement.

evidence.quote: A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42). A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42. A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class.
Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes. Whitespace and comments are usually skipped while line/column positions are retained.

A parse tree shows grammar productions: root S, internal nonterminals, and terminal leaves, with ε sometimes shown for empty productions. Its left-to-right yield is the input. An AST omits grammar scaffolding and punctuation; expression operands are leaves and operators internal nodes. The parser can build either representation, depending on implementation.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of a symbol table?
questions.hint: Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens.

answer.text: A symbol table associates names with declaration attributes.
answer.explanation: COMP19 maps names or identities to type, scope, width, offsets, signatures and linkage information. These records support declaration lookup and semantic checks; a hash table is one implementation rather than the purpose itself.

evidence.quote: A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage. A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting. Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.

Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type. Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal. Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table. A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.

questions.stem: What is the difference between top-down and bottom-up parsing?
questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Top-down expands from the start symbol; bottom-up reduces input toward it.
answer.explanation: COMP15 describes bottom-up recognition as input reductions toward S, reversing a rightmost derivation. COMP11 describes top-down expansion from S toward the input, normally a leftmost derivation.

evidence.quote: Top-down parsing starts with S and expands productions toward the input, usually constructing a leftmost derivation. Recursive descent typically has one procedure per nonterminal. A general recursive-descent implementation can backtrack; a predictive parser chooses a production using lookahead without backtracking. LL(1) scans Left to right, produces a Leftmost derivation and uses one lookahead token.

Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse. A handle is a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next step of that reverse derivation. Not every substring matching a RHS is a handle in the current context.

questions.stem: What is intermediate code and why is it used?
questions.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.

answer.text: IR separates source analysis from target lowering and enables reuse.
answer.explanation: COMP26 defines IR’s role in separating source meaning from target implementation so analysis, optimization and backends can be reused. ASTs, graphs, TAC and bytecode are possible forms. A useful IR is easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower; portability does not require every IR to exclude all target-specific details.

evidence.quote: IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a valid token type produced during lexical analysis?
questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Parse-tree node is not a lexical token type.
answer.explanation: COMP04 lists keywords, identifiers and literals among token classes. A parse-tree node belongs to the grammatical structure built after scanning, not the lexical class of a source lexeme. Consequently only parse-tree node is the invalid token-type choice, while the other three are ordinary scanner output categories.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Keywords are explicitly listed as a valid lexical token class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Parse-tree nodes represent grammatical structure, not a lexical token category emitted by a scanner.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Identifiers are an ordinary lexical token class.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Numeric literals are literals and therefore valid token categories.

evidence.quote: A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42). A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42. A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class. The scanner emits an ordered token stream, not an unordered mathematical set.

Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes. Whitespace and comments are usually skipped while line/column positions are retained. In indentation-sensitive or newline-sensitive languages, layout can carry tokens. Parse-tree construction is a parser task; scanning can intern identifier spellings, but declaration scope and types need later analysis.

questions.stem: What algorithm is commonly used to convert a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) to a Deterministic Finite Automaton (DFA) in lexer construction?
questions.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.

answer.explanation: COMP06 distinguishes Thompson construction, which builds an NFA from a regular expression, from subset construction, which determinizes the NFA. Each DFA state represents an NFA-state subset, with epsilon closure when needed. CYK and Earley are grammar-parsing algorithms rather than this automaton determinization, so the powerset option is the relevant stage.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thompson construction goes from regular expression to NFA rather than NFA to DFA.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Subset construction creates DFA states from sets of NFA states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: CYK performs CFG membership parsing and does not determinize a lexical NFA.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Earley is a grammar-parsing method rather than the stated NFA-to-DFA construction.

evidence.quote: A common generator pipeline is regular expressions → NFA using Thompson construction → DFA using subset construction; minimization is optional.

The ε-closure of states includes those reachable by zero or more ε edges. A DFA state is a set of NFA states; its a-transition is ε-closure(move(set,a)). Start with the NFA start closure, repeatedly add unseen subsets, and mark subsets containing an NFA final state as accepting. Token identity and rule priority annotate accepting states; the empty subset acts as a dead state.

CYK and Earley are context-free grammar parsing algorithms. They determine grammatical structure or membership of an input sequence. They are different tasks from Thompson construction, which builds a token-recognizing NFA from a regular expression, and subset construction, which turns an NFA into a DFA.

questions.stem: Given the grammar:  E → E + T | T,  T → T * F | F,  F → (E) | id — this grammar enforces:

options.label: B
options.text: Left-associativity for both + and *, with * having higher precedence than +

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Both operators associate left; multiplication has higher precedence.
answer.explanation: COMP10 states exactly these productions and their effect. Multiplication occurs within T below the addition level E, so it binds more tightly. The recursive operand on the left of E→E+T and T→T*F enforces left association for each operator. Parentheses in F can override the default grouping.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The recursive nonterminal is on the left, producing left rather than right association.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Separate T multiplication and E addition levels give higher multiplication precedence and left association.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Addition is left-recursive too, so it does not have the claimed right association.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The grammar explicitly encodes both precedence levels and associativity.

evidence.quote: Use E→E+T|T, T→T*F|F, F→(E)|id to give * higher precedence and both operators left associativity. For subtraction, a−b−c then groups (a−b)−c.

questions.stem: For a reduced CFG (all symbols reachable and productive), which conditions prevent it from being LL(1)? Select all that apply. In A, overlap means a shared terminal in competing RHS FIRST sets.

options.label: A
options.text: Two productions for the same non-terminal have overlapping FIRST sets |

options.label: B
options.text: The grammar contains a left-recursive rule

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Two productions for the same non-terminal have overlapping FIRST sets |; The grammar contains a left-recursive rule; The grammar is ambiguous |
answer.explanation: A shared FIRST terminal for alternatives of one nonterminal creates a predictive-table collision. Reachable left recursion prevents ordinary LL(1) prediction, and an ambiguous useful grammar cannot have a unique LL(1) parse. Thus A, B and C are all obstructions. The combined D alternative wrongly says only A and B, excluding ambiguity, so it is not a complete correct selection.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Shared FIRST terminals create competing table entries.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reachable left recursion rules out ordinary LL(1) parsing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A useful ambiguous grammar is not LL(1).

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The word only wrongly excludes the valid ambiguity obstruction.

evidence.quote: For every A→α, put it in M[A,a] for each terminal a in FIRST(α). If α is nullable, also enter it under every symbol in FOLLOW(A). More than one production in a cell is a conflict. Pairwise SELECT sets must be disjoint; SELECT(α)=FIRST(α)−{ε}, plus FOLLOW(A) when α is nullable. This also detects two nullable alternatives.
Indirect left recursion follows a cycle through other nonterminals and also needs removal for ordinary predictive descent.
LR parsers can handle suitable left-recursive grammars; ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever before consuming input.
Deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous; a general ambiguous grammar requires rewriting, disambiguation policy or a generalized method such as GLR.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a synthesized attribute in attribute grammars?

options.label: A
options.text: The type of an expression computed from its sub-expressions |

options.label: B
options.text: The scope environment passed down to a block

options.label: C
options.text: The inherited type context for a function body |

options.label: D
options.text: The enclosing loop level passed to a break statement

questions.hint: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information.

answer.text: Expression type computed from subexpressions is synthesized.
answer.explanation: COMP24 defines synthesized attributes by flow from children to a parent. Computing an expression’s type from its subexpressions fits this direction. Scope, type context and enclosing-loop information passed down from surrounding constructs instead supply inherited context. The direction of dependency, rather than the fact that types are involved, distinguishes these choices.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The parent expression derives its type from child subexpressions, which is synthesized upward flow.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A scope environment passed down to a block is inherited contextual information.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A type context supplied to a function body flows from its surroundings, so it is inherited.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Enclosing-loop context is passed inward to a break statement rather than synthesized from its children.

evidence.quote: A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions. An annotated parse tree displays computed attribute values; it is not itself an inherited or synthesized attribute. Synthesized attributes flow from children to a parent; inherited attributes carry context from parent or siblings.

For E→E1+T, E.val=E1.val+T.val synthesizes an expression value. A declaration’s type environment passed into its body is inherited. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit LR reduction-time evaluation naturally; suitable LL parsers can also compute them. L-attributed definitions restrict dependencies so a left-to-right traversal can evaluate inherited context. Attribute dependency cycles can prevent evaluation.

questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of Three-Address Code (TAC) as an intermediate representation?

options.label: A
options.text: To directly execute on the target CPU |

options.label: B
options.text: To provide a machine-independent representation suitable for optimization and code generation

questions.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.

answer.text: An optimization-friendly intermediate representation for later target generation.
answer.explanation: COMP26 gives reuse and separation as the purpose of IR and describes TAC as simple instruction records. TAC is normally not directly executed by a native CPU, does not replace declaration metadata and is not limited to arithmetic: branches and assignments are also representable. B states its architectural optimization/code-generation role most directly.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: TAC is normally intermediate and requires lowering rather than direct execution on the target CPU.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TAC provides analyzable intermediate operations supporting reuse, optimization and later target-code generation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A symbol table retains declaration metadata and is not replaced by the instruction representation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: TAC can encode control transfers and other operations, not only arithmetic expressions.

evidence.quote: IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused. It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.

Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2. Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions. Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement. Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.

questions.stem: The 'maximal munch' rule in lexical analysis means:

options.label: A
options.text: The lexer always produces the shortest possible token |

options.label: B
options.text: The lexer always produces the longest possible token matching the current position

options.label: C
options.text: Keyword tokens are prioritized over identifiers |

options.label: D
options.text: Comments are included in the token stream

questions.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.

answer.text: Choose the longest matching lexeme at the current position.
answer.explanation: COMP07 defines longest matching lexeme selection at each input position. Equal-length matches use rule order, which is a separate tie-breaking rule; keywords do not override a longer identifier such as ifx. Comments are normally skipped rather than retained merely because maximal munch is used. This establishes B as the definition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Shortest-match selection is the opposite of maximal munch.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The lexer consumes the longest available match beginning at the current input position.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Keyword priority can break equal-length rule ties but does not define longest match.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Comment retention is independent of longest match; ordinary comments are skipped.

evidence.quote: At each input position, choose the longest matching lexeme; if equal lengths match multiple flex rules, choose the earliest rule. Thus ifx is an identifier rather than if followed by x; <= and ++ are each one operator token. An implementation may recognize an identifier first and then consult a keyword table.

questions.stem: In bottom-up parsing, a 'shift-reduce conflict' occurs when:

options.label: A
options.text: There are two possible reductions for the same stack top |

options.label: B
options.text: The parser cannot decide whether to shift the next input token or reduce the current stack contents

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: A competing shift and reduction on the same situation.
answer.explanation: COMP17 defines a shift/reduce conflict as a choice between consuming a token and reducing. Two competing reductions describe reduce/reduce instead. Left recursion may be entirely acceptable to LR, and an empty FOLLOW set is not the definition of this table conflict. The conflict concerns competing actions for the same state and lookahead.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Two possible reductions define a reduce/reduce conflict, a different conflict type.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The same parser situation permits both shifting input and reducing the recognized right-hand side.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: LR can handle suitable left recursion; that property does not itself define a shift/reduce conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FOLLOW-set emptiness does not express competing shift and reduction actions.

evidence.quote: SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items. LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts. The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.

A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous. Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG. Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.

questions.stem: Which optimization technique moves loop-invariant computations outside the loop body?
questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.explanation: COMP32 explains that an expression whose inputs remain unchanged can be moved to a preheader when safe on newly executed paths. That is loop-invariant code motion. Strength reduction changes operation cost, unrolling replicates the body, and dead-code elimination removes unused or unreachable work. Hoisting also requires safety, not merely unchanged operands.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Strength reduction substitutes a cheaper equivalent operation rather than necessarily moving it outside a loop.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Unrolling replicates loop bodies instead of hoisting invariant computations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: LICM moves invariant computations to an appropriate outside location when executing them there is safe.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Dead-code elimination removes unnecessary computations rather than relocating a needed invariant value.

evidence.quote: A loop-invariant expression has unchanged inputs during a loop. Hoist it to a preheader only when evaluation is safe on the paths where it will newly run. Induction variables change by a loop-invariant increment, such as i=i+1. For repeated t=4*i, maintain a running t increased by 4 when equivalent, reducing repeated multiplication.

Loop fusion or jamming combines loops with compatible bounds and safe dependence order. Unrolling replicates a body to reduce branch overhead and expose parallelism; handle remaining iterations and increased code size. Loop-invariant code motion, fusion, unrolling and strength reduction are different transformations. A finite taxonomy needs a criterion: machine dependent/independent versus local/global/loop are different classifications.

questions.stem: What does 'register spilling' mean in the context of register allocation?

options.label: A
options.text: Allocating the same register to two variables |

options.label: B
options.text: Storing a variable in memory instead of a register because no register is available

options.label: C
options.text: Using floating-point registers for integer values |

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: Store selected values in memory and insert loads/stores when registers do not suffice.
answer.explanation: COMP36 says spilling places selected values in memory when the register assignment cannot fit available registers. Loads and stores then connect memory-resident values to instructions needing registers. Register sharing can be legal for nonoverlapping live ranges, while copy elimination and choosing a different register class are separate operations rather than this storage fallback.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Register sharing may be legal for disjoint live ranges and does not itself describe spilling.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Spilling moves selected values to memory because a feasible register-only assignment is unavailable.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Using another register class is not the definition of writing spilled values to memory.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Removing redundant register copies is a different optimization from memory-backed spilling.

evidence.quote: A value is live where it can be used before redefinition. In the interference model, values that must coexist in distinct registers are connected by an edge; each register is a color. Nonoverlapping live ranges may share a register. If a valid assignment cannot fit the available registers, spilling places selected values in memory and inserts loads/stores.

The general graph k-colorability decision problem is NP-complete for fixed k≥3; optimal register assignment/spill minimization is a hard optimization problem in general, so practical allocators use heuristics.

questions.stem: For Java numeric conversions such as int→long and int→float, which statement correctly describes widening?

options.label: A
options.text: Converting a wider type to a narrower type, possibly losing information |

options.label: B
options.text: Converting to a numeric type with a wider representable range; some widening conversions can still lose precision.

options.label: C
options.text: Declaring a variable with an explicit type annotation |

options.label: D
options.text: Assigning a value to a pointer of a different type

questions.hint: Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning.

answer.text: Converting to a numeric type with a wider representable range; some widening conversions can still lose precision.
answer.explanation: Java int→long is widening and exact, while int→float is also widening even though some large integer values round. Widening therefore does not universally guarantee preservation of every bit of precision. Narrowing goes toward a more restricted representation; type annotations and arbitrary pointer changes are separate concepts. Option B captures the relevant larger-range conversion without making the false no-loss promise.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This describes narrowing rather than widening.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Widening can increase range while still losing precision, as int→float illustrates.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An explicit annotation declares a type rather than converting a value.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An arbitrary pointer-type change does not define Java numeric widening.

evidence.quote: Coercion is an implicit conversion permitted by the language; a cast requests an explicit conversion. Widening often increases representable range, but can still lose precision: Java int→float is widening although large integers round. Java int→long is exact. Narrowing can lose range or fractional information.

In C++ ordinary int x=3.14 converts to 3 when representable; it is not inherently a type error. int x{3.14} is rejected as narrowing. C++ floating-to-integer conversion discards the fraction and has undefined behavior if the truncated value is unrepresentable. Java ordinary double→int assignment needs a permitted explicit cast. Mixing char and int is ordinarily valid after promotion in C++/Java; do not import a fictitious universal ban.

questions.stem: Which of the following data structures is most commonly used to implement a symbol table for fast insertion and lookup?
questions.hint: Ask whether the required information is a declaration’s identity and attributes, program structure or the ordered source tokens.

answer.explanation: COMP19 directly identifies hashing as giving expected constant-time insertion and lookup under suitable hashing. A stack supports nested scope order but is not the primary keyed mapping. Lists and trees are possible alternatives, yet neither is the specific common expected-constant-time structure emphasized in the note and requested by the stem.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A sorted linked list generally requires linear search and does not supply the highlighted expected constant lookup.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Hash tables commonly implement expected O(1) symbol insertion and lookup.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A search tree is possible, but the note specifically identifies hashing for the usual fast keyed implementation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A stack organizes scope nesting rather than providing fast arbitrary name lookup within a scope.

evidence.quote: A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage. A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting. Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.

Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type. Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal. Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table. A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.

questions.stem: A grammar is said to be 'left-factored' when:

options.label: B
options.text: Productions for the same non-terminal that share a common prefix are rewritten to factor out the prefix

options.label: D
options.text: The grammar can be parsed by a bottom-up parser only

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Common prefixes are factored out of alternatives.
answer.explanation: COMP12 rewrites A→αβ|αγ as A→αA′ and A′→β|γ. The transformation postpones the alternative choice until after consuming the common prefix. It does not mean making productions left-recursive, removing all epsilon rules or restricting parsing to bottom-up methods; left factoring alone also does not guarantee LL(1).

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Left recursion and left factoring are distinct properties and transformations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Factoring extracts shared prefixes and delays selection between the remaining suffix alternatives.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Factoring does not require removing every epsilon production.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Factored grammars can support top-down prediction; bottom-up exclusivity is not a defining condition.

evidence.quote:
Left factoring rewrites A→αβ|αγ using:
A→αA′
A′→β|γ
It postpones a choice until after the common prefix. It does not by itself remove ambiguity or guarantee LL(1). LR parsers can handle suitable left-recursive grammars; ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever before consuming input.

questions.stem: What is 'constant propagation' in compiler optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Evaluating constant expressions at compile time |

options.label: B
options.text: Replacing uses of a variable with its known constant value at each program point

options.label: C
options.text: Removing code that has no effect on program output |

options.label: D
options.text: Moving constants from memory to registers

questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.text: Replace uses with their known constant values.
answer.explanation: COMP30 gives x=3; y=x+2 becoming y=3+2 before folding. Replacing x by its known value is propagation; evaluating 3+2 is folding. Removing unnecessary code or choosing register locations addresses different transformations. The program-point qualification matters because the value must still be known on all relevant incoming paths.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Evaluating an already constant expression is constant folding, which can follow propagation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Propagation substitutes a variable’s established constant value at uses where that fact holds.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Removing effect-free unused or unreachable work is dead-code elimination.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Memory-to-register placement is not the substitution of a known compile-time value.

evidence.quote: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions during compilation: 3*4→12. Constant propagation substitutes known values: x=3; y=x+2 becomes y=3+2 before folding. Copy propagation substitutes a copied name while its source remains unchanged. Dead-code elimination removes unreachable code or computations whose values are unused and whose evaluation has no necessary side effects.

questions.stem: In an LR parsing table, what does a 'reduce/reduce conflict' indicate?

options.label: A
options.text: Two different productions can both be used to reduce the same stack contents with the same lookahead |

options.label: B
options.text: The parser must both shift and reduce on the same input symbol

options.label: C
options.text: The grammar has a dangling else problem |

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Two competing reductions for the same parser state/lookahead.
answer.explanation: COMP17 defines reduce/reduce as two reductions being available. In a parsing table that means the same state and lookahead permit different completed productions. A shift competing with reduction is another conflict type. Dangling else is a grammar ambiguity example, and epsilon productions alone do not guarantee any reduce/reduce collision.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The table offers two different production reductions for the same state and lookahead.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Simultaneous shift and reduce actions define shift/reduce rather than reduce/reduce.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Dangling else commonly creates an attachment ambiguity, not the definition of two competing reductions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Epsilon rules can appear in conflict-free grammars and do not alone imply this collision.

evidence.quote: SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items. LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts. The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.

A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous. Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG. Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.

questions.stem: Which compiler phase is primarily responsible for detecting the incompatible assignment in the Java declaration int x = "hello";?
questions.hint: Check operand compatibility and permitted conversions under the stated language rules; distinguish grammatical structure from semantic meaning.

answer.explanation: The declaration has recognizable tokens and a valid declaration-shaped syntax, but assigns a string to an integer variable. Under Java’s type rules this violates assignment compatibility, so semantic analysis and type checking identify the error. Scanning recognizes the identifier, type keyword and literal; parsing organizes them. Code generation uses the checked representation later. The named language removes any assumption that every statically typed language has identical implicit conversions.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The individual tokens are recognizable; the error is their type compatibility.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The declaration’s grammar structure is not the primary problem.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Semantic type checking rejects the string-to-integer assignment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Code generation follows the frontend type check rather than defining this compatibility rule.

evidence.quote: A lexical error prevents forming a legal token, such as an invalid character or unterminated literal. A syntax error is an illegal token arrangement, such as a missing delimiter. A semantic error violates name, scope or type rules after grammatical recognition. A wrong algorithm can compile successfully; compilers do not detect all logical mistakes.
int x="hello" is a type mismatch in ordinary C++/Java; division by zero and bounds violations are not automatically operand-type mismatches.

questions.stem: In Thompson's construction for building an NFA from a regular expression, the NFA for the concatenation r1r2 is built by:

options.label: A
options.text: Merging the start states of both NFAs |

options.label: B
options.text: Adding an ε-transition from the accepting state(s) of the NFA for r1 to the start state of the NFA for r2

options.label: C
options.text: Creating a new start state with ε-transitions to both NFAs |

options.label: D
options.text: Taking the cross product of the two NFAs

questions.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.

answer.text: Connect the first fragment’s accepting end to the second start with ε.
answer.explanation: COMP06 directly gives the concatenation rule: connect r’s final state to s’s start by epsilon. This forces any complete path through the first fragment to continue through the second in order. Branching epsilon paths instead implement alternation; merged starts and product constructions do not implement the specified Thompson concatenation step.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Merging starts does not force a complete r1 match followed by an r2 match.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The epsilon connection joins the first accepting end to the second start without consuming input.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A new branching start with epsilon alternatives implements union rather than concatenation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A state cross product is not the Thompson fragment connection for concatenation.

evidence.quote: A common generator pipeline is regular expressions → NFA using Thompson construction → DFA using subset construction; minimization is optional. For concatenation rs, connect r’s final state to s’s start by ε. Alternation introduces branching ε paths; star adds a way to skip and repeat the fragment.

The ε-closure of states includes those reachable by zero or more ε edges. A DFA state is a set of NFA states; its a-transition is ε-closure(move(set,a)). Start with the NFA start closure, repeatedly add unseen subsets, and mark subsets containing an NFA final state as accepting. Token identity and rule priority annotate accepting states; the empty subset acts as a dead state.

questions.stem: What is the 'dangling else' problem?

options.label: A
options.text: An else branch that can never be reached due to preceding conditions |

options.label: B
options.text: Ambiguity in grammars that allows an else to be matched with either of two if statements

options.label: C
options.text: An else clause that lacks a body |

options.label: D
options.text: An else used outside an if statement

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Ambiguous attachment of else to one of two nested ifs.
answer.explanation: COMP10 describes an else that can attach to either nested if and resolves it with nearest-unmatched-if policy or a grammar rewrite. That grammatical ambiguity is the dangling-else problem. It does not mean unreachable code, a missing body or an else outside any if, which are different semantic or syntactic situations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Unreachability concerns control-flow feasibility, not the competing grammatical attachment of else.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The ambiguity is whether else belongs to the inner or outer unmatched if.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A missing else body is a syntax defect rather than the classic attachment ambiguity.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An else outside any if is not the two-attachment situation defining dangling else.

evidence.quote: The dangling-else grammar permits else to attach to either nested if; a nearest-unmatched-if rule or grammar rewrite resolves it. Taking a leftmost derivation by itself does not resolve ambiguous interpretation.

questions.stem: Which representation explicitly uses basic blocks as vertices and possible transfers as edges, making it the direct structural basis for dominator and natural-loop analysis?
questions.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.

answer.explanation: A control-flow graph explicitly records basic blocks and their possible successor transfers. Dominator relationships describe which blocks occur on every path to another block; back edges to dominating headers identify natural loops. TAC can populate the blocks, and SSA can coexist with this graph, but neither alone names the requested vertex/edge structure. An AST emphasizes source syntax rather than this control-flow representation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: An AST represents source hierarchy rather than the specified block-transfer graph.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: TAC gives instructions, not by itself the requested graph.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SSA is a definition-naming discipline that can coexist with a CFG.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A CFG explicitly provides the specified blocks, edges and path structure.

evidence.quote: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence entered at its beginning and exited at its end. Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and each instruction after a branch. Start a block at each leader and continue until the next leader.

A control-flow graph has blocks as vertices and possible next-block transfers as edges, including fall-through. A node D dominates N when every entry-to-N path passes through D. For an edge N→H where H dominates N, H is a loop header of a natural loop. This structure supports loop analysis. An expression DAG records value dependencies, not arbitrary control flow.

questions.stem: In Static Single Assignment (SSA) form, what is the purpose of a 'φ (phi) function'?

options.label: A
options.text: To represent a conditional branch in the control flow graph |

options.label: B
options.text: To select the correct version of a variable at join points where multiple control flow paths merge

options.label: C
options.text: To mark the entry point of a function |

options.label: D
options.text: To represent a loop-back edge in the CFG

questions.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.

answer.text: Select the incoming variable version corresponding to the predecessor taken.
answer.explanation: COMP27 defines phi at a join as choosing an incoming value according to the actual predecessor path. It is not a conditional branch instruction, a function-entry marker or a back edge, and does not average its operands. The function reconciles distinct definition names when different paths reach the same use.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A phi function selects an incoming value; it does not transfer control between blocks.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: It merges definition versions by selecting the value associated with the predecessor actually taken.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Function entry is a control-flow location, not the value-selection purpose of phi.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A back edge represents loop control transfer rather than a merge of SSA values.

evidence.quote: A conditional expression can generate if a<b goto Ltrue; goto Lfalse; labels join control paths. Short-circuit AND evaluates the right operand only after a true left operand; OR only after a false one. Translating both eagerly can change side effects. For a zero-based array with element width w and lower bound L, element i uses base+(i−L)*w, assuming fixed-width contiguous storage.

SSA gives each definition a distinct name. At a join, x3=φ(x1 from B1,x2 from B2) chooses the incoming value according to the predecessor actually taken; it is not an arithmetic average. SSA is a naming discipline over IR and commonly coexists with a control-flow graph.

questions.stem: The FOLLOW set of the start symbol S always contains:

options.label: C
options.text: The first terminal of every production |

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.explanation: COMP13 explicitly places $ in FOLLOW(S), representing that a completed start-symbol derivation can be followed by end of input. FOLLOW never contains epsilon. Possible initial terminals belong to FIRST, not automatically FOLLOW. Therefore the marker is guaranteed even when other following terminals depend on the grammar.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FOLLOW contains terminals and possibly the end marker, never epsilon.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The end-of-input marker is placed in FOLLOW of the start symbol by initialization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Initial terminals are FIRST information and are not automatically following terminals.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FOLLOW(S) is not empty because it contains the end marker.

evidence.quote: FIRST(α) contains terminals that can begin strings derived from α, plus ε when α can vanish. For a sequence, add FIRST of each symbol except ε, continue while symbols are nullable, and add ε only if every symbol is nullable.

FOLLOW(A) contains possible next terminals after A, plus end marker $ where appropriate; never ε. Put $ in FOLLOW(S). For B→αAβ, add FIRST(β)−{ε} to FOLLOW(A); if β is nullable, add FOLLOW(B). Repeat all rules until no sets grow.

questions.stem: For an unsigned fixed-width integer x with width greater than three and modular arithmetic, which optimization replaces x = x * 8 with x = x << 3?
questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.explanation: The transformation replaces multiplication by a power of two with an equivalent shift under the stated unsigned model. This is strength reduction when the target makes that replacement cheaper. It does not evaluate a constant-only expression because x remains variable, does not remove an unused statement, and does not replicate loop iterations. The explicit arithmetic model matters because signed-language overflow or shift rules can make a superficially similar rewrite invalid.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The operand x remains variable, so this is not evaluation of an all-constant expression.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The assignment remains and still computes a needed result.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Replacing an operation by an equivalent cheaper form is strength reduction.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No loop body is replicated.

evidence.quote: Algebraic simplification removes identities when valid: integer x+0→x. Strength reduction replaces an operation with an equivalent cheaper form, such as unsigned x*8→x<<3 for a valid width and shift count. Target costs determine whether it is actually cheaper.
Signed C/C++ overflow and shift rules differ from unsigned modular arithmetic; a mathematical identity is not automatically a legal transformation.
Unrolling replicates a body to reduce branch overhead and expose parallelism; handle remaining iterations and increased code size.

questions.stem: In a compiler's code generator, 'calling convention' refers to:

options.label: A
options.text: The order in which source files are compiled |

options.label: B
options.text: The agreed-upon protocol for how functions pass arguments, return values, and manage the stack

options.label: C
options.text: The naming convention for generated labels |

options.label: D
options.text: The format of debug information in the object file

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: The protocol for arguments, results, registers and stack management.
answer.explanation: COMP37 defines the locations of arguments/results, saved-register responsibilities, stack alignment and frame duties as the calling convention. These permit caller and callee to agree on the runtime call interface. Source-file build order, label spelling and debug format concern other compiler/toolchain conventions rather than this execution protocol.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Compilation order concerns build organization rather than the runtime interface between callers and callees.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The calling convention specifies argument/result passing and register/stack responsibilities.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Label naming is separate from the runtime storage and control-transfer call protocol.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Debug information format is not the protocol used to invoke and return from functions.

evidence.quote: Static storage lasts throughout execution; stack frames support nested calls and recursion; heap storage supports lifetimes beyond a call. A frame may contain parameters, return address, saved registers, locals and temporaries. Sizes, alignment and offsets are target-dependent; a two-byte int is an example, not a C++ guarantee.

A calling convention specifies argument and result locations, caller/callee-saved registers, stack alignment and frame responsibilities. Escape analysis asks whether an object/reference can outlive or be accessed outside a region such as its allocating call. Proven nonescaping allocations may use stack storage or be eliminated by scalar replacement, provided identity and lifetime semantics remain correct.

questions.stem: What does 'peephole optimization' involve?

options.label: B
options.text: Examining and replacing small sequences of generated instructions with more efficient equivalents

options.label: C
options.text: Inlining small functions at call sites |

questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.text: Examine short instruction sequences and replace them with better equivalents.
answer.explanation: COMP31 defines peephole optimization by short instruction windows and lists redundant-load removal, machine idioms and jump-chain shortening. B states that method directly. Whole-function optimization has a broader scope; inlining changes calls to bodies, and unreachable-block removal is a particular control-flow simplification rather than the definition of examining small windows.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Whole-function scope is broader than the short instruction windows defining peephole optimization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The optimizer inspects short instruction sequences and substitutes equivalent more efficient forms.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Inlining expands calls into bodies rather than defining the local instruction-window method.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Unreachable-block removal is one control-flow optimization, not the defining peephole inspection mechanism.

evidence.quote: Peephole optimization examines short instruction windows. It can remove redundant loads/stores, replace machine idioms and shorten jump chains: jump L1 where L1 immediately jumps L2 can become jump L2.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares LALR(1) with SLR(1) and canonical LR(1), allowing the case where no equal-core canonical states need merging?

options.label: B
options.text: LALR(1) has no more states than canonical LR(1) and can resolve some conflicts SLR(1) cannot.

options.label: C
options.text: LALR(1) and SLR(1) produce identical parsing tables for all grammars |

options.label: D
options.text: LALR(1) requires more lookahead than SLR(1)

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: LALR(1) has no more states than canonical LR(1) and can resolve some conflicts SLR(1) cannot.
answer.explanation: LALR combines lookaheads of canonical LR(1) states with equal LR(0) cores. This gives no more states than the canonical machine, with a reduction when distinct equal-core states merge. LALR can handle some grammars beyond SLR because its lookaheads are more precise. Both use one lookahead token, and their tables are not identical for every grammar.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The hierarchy places SLR within LALR rather than the reverse.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This states both the correct state-count bound and the greater parsing capability.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The methods can use different reduction lookaheads and tables.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both use one lookahead token.

evidence.quote: SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items. LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts. The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.

A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous. Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG. Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.

questions.stem: In data flow analysis, 'live variable analysis' is a:
questions.hint: Track which facts can hold along one path and which must hold along every path. Apply the specified direction, transfer rule and join operation.

answer.explanation: COMP29 explicitly calls liveness backward may-analysis. A value is live if some future path reads it before redefinition, so information flows backward from successor uses and combines possible uses rather than requiring every path. This distinguishes both the direction and may-versus-must dimensions requested by the options.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: May is appropriate, but liveness propagates from future uses backward rather than forward.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Liveness asks whether some future path uses a value before redefinition, a backward may property.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Both direction and must quantification differ from the liveness definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Backward direction fits, but liveness requires a possible use, not use on every path.

evidence.quote: Liveness is backward may-analysis: a value might be read before redefinition on some future path. OUT[B]=union of IN over successors; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]). Iterate to a fixed point. Liveness supports register allocation and dead-value removal. Definite-assignment analysis asks whether initialization occurs on every path before use; reaching definitions alone does not prove this.

questions.stem: The 'closure' operation in NFA-to-DFA subset construction computes:

options.label: A
options.text: The set of all NFA states reachable from a given set of states using only ε-transitions |

options.label: B
options.text: The set of all NFA states reachable using any number of any transitions

options.label: C
options.text: The minimal DFA equivalent to the NFA |

options.label: D
options.text: The FIRST set of a non-terminal

questions.hint: Follow the representation at each construction step and apply the pattern or state-set rules consistently, including empty cases.

answer.text: States reachable by zero or more ε transitions.
answer.explanation: COMP06 defines epsilon closure as all states reachable without consuming input through zero or more epsilon edges. Zero moves includes the starting set itself. Arbitrary labeled transitions would consume symbols and belong to a different reachability relation; minimization and FIRST-set computation are separate algorithms. A therefore matches the closure used in subset construction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Epsilon closure includes the starting set and every state reachable using only epsilon edges.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Arbitrary symbol transitions consume input and are not part of epsilon closure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Closure supplies subsets during determinization; it does not itself minimize the resulting DFA.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FIRST is a grammar lookahead set, not epsilon reachability among NFA states.

evidence.quote: A common generator pipeline is regular expressions → NFA using Thompson construction → DFA using subset construction; minimization is optional. For concatenation rs, connect r’s final state to s’s start by ε. Alternation introduces branching ε paths; star adds a way to skip and repeat the fragment.

The ε-closure of states includes those reachable by zero or more ε edges. A DFA state is a set of NFA states; its a-transition is ε-closure(move(set,a)). Start with the NFA start closure, repeatedly add unseen subsets, and mark subsets containing an NFA final state as accepting. Token identity and rule priority annotate accepting states; the empty subset acts as a dead state.

questions.stem: For a real-machine backend, which listed optimization chiefly depends on the target’s instruction latencies and execution resources?
questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.explanation: Instruction scheduling chooses a legal instruction order while considering target resources and latencies. It is therefore the target-dependent backend choice in this comparison. Constant folding computes known expressions, dead-code elimination removes unnecessary computation while preserving effects, and loop-invariant motion relocates safe unchanged expressions. Their validity depends on program semantics, but these three need not be organized around a particular processor’s scheduling resources.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Folding evaluates known expressions from program semantics rather than scheduling machine resources.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Dead-code elimination uses reachability, use and side-effect information.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Instruction scheduling considers target execution resources and instruction latencies.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Invariant motion uses loop values, paths and safety conditions rather than target issue scheduling.

evidence.quote: Instruction scheduling orders selected target instructions while preserving dependencies. A target-aware scheduler also considers instruction latencies and the processor resources needed by each operation. This is a backend optimization whose performance choices depend on the target machine, even when a reusable scheduling framework serves many targets.

By contrast, constant folding, dead-code elimination and safe loop-invariant motion can be expressed on a target-neutral IR using values, control flow and side-effect rules. Target costs can still influence whether a legal transformation is worthwhile. Machine independence therefore describes the abstraction of a pass, not freedom from all language semantics or implementation costs.

questions.stem: In a context-free grammar, a 'sentential form' is:

options.label: A
options.text: A string consisting only of terminal symbols |

options.label: B
options.text: Any string of terminals and non-terminals derivable from the start symbol

options.label: C
options.text: A string that cannot be further reduced |

options.label: D
options.text: The right-hand side of a production rule

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Any terminal/nonterminal string derivable from the start symbol.
answer.explanation: COMP09 defines a sentential form as any string of terminals and nonterminals derivable from S. Terminal-only sentences are a special case, not the full definition. A production right side need not itself be reachable from S, and irreducibility does not define derivability. B captures the required reachability and permits both kinds of symbols.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Terminal-only strings are sentences, a subset of sentential forms rather than their full definition.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Derivability from the start symbol with terminals and possibly nonterminals is the defining property.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A sentential form can still contain expandable nonterminals; inability to reduce is not required.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A right-hand side is not necessarily reachable from the grammar’s start symbol.

evidence.quote: A context-free grammar G=(N,T,P,S) has nonterminals N, terminals T, productions P and start S. A production A→α rewrites one nonterminal. A sentential form is any string of terminals/nonterminals derivable from S; a sentence contains only terminals. A leftmost derivation rewrites the leftmost remaining nonterminal; a rightmost one rewrites the rightmost.

A parse tree shows grammar productions: root S, internal nonterminals, and terminal leaves, with ε sometimes shown for empty productions. Its left-to-right yield is the input. An AST omits grammar scaffolding and punctuation; expression operands are leaves and operators internal nodes. The parser can build either representation, depending on implementation.

questions.stem: What is 'function inlining' and what is its primary risk?

options.label: A
options.text: Replacing a function call with the function body; risk is incorrect semantics |

options.label: B
options.text: Replacing a function call with the function body; risk is increased code size (code bloat)

options.label: C
options.text: Moving a function to a different module; risk is linker errors |

options.label: D
options.text: Specializing a function for specific argument values; risk is type errors

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: Replace a call with its body; excessive code size is a risk.
answer.explanation: COMP38 defines inlining as substituting a suitably renamed body while preserving argument evaluation, returns and side effects. It can remove call overhead but increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. Correct inlining preserves semantics; corruption is an implementation bug rather than its defining trade-off. Moving modules or specializing arguments describes different transformations.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Inlining must preserve semantics; incorrect behavior is a bug rather than the normal primary trade-off stated here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Body substitution can reduce call overhead while increasing generated code size.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Moving a function between modules is not call-site body substitution.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Argument specialization is a different optimization and does not define general function inlining.

evidence.quote: Inlining replaces a call with a suitably renamed copy of its body, preserving argument evaluation, returns and side effects. It can remove call overhead and expose optimization opportunities, but may increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. A recursive function cannot simply be expanded without limit.

Virtual dispatch chooses an overridden method based on a receiver’s runtime class. A common implementation uses a per-class virtual-method table and an object pointer to the table; the call loads the selected entry. This is an implementation strategy, not a universal language requirement. Name mangling distinguishes linker symbols, often for overloads; it is not itself runtime method selection. Proven receiver types may permit devirtualization.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the 'handle' in bottom-up parsing?

options.label: A
options.text: The leftmost terminal in the input string |

options.label: B
options.text: A substring of the current sentential form that matches the right-hand side of a production and whose reduction leads to a valid parse

options.label: C
options.text: The top element of the parsing stack |

options.label: D
options.text: The lookahead token used for parsing decisions

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: The RHS occurrence whose next reverse-rightmost reduction leads toward the valid parse.
answer.explanation: COMP15 defines a handle as a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next reverse-rightmost derivation step. B is the closest complete description: its valid-parse condition must mean that next legitimate step, not merely any matching substring. Neither a single stack item nor the lookahead alone specifies that contextual production occurrence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The leftmost terminal need not be the handle and does not identify a production RHS occurrence.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Read valid reduction as the next reverse-rightmost step; contextual validity distinguishes a handle from arbitrary matches.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A handle can span multiple symbols and is not simply the top stack element.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Lookahead guides action selection but is not the substring being reduced.

evidence.quote: Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse. A handle is a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next step of that reverse derivation. Not every substring matching a RHS is a handle in the current context.

Shift pushes the next input token and a state; reduce replaces a recognized RHS by its LHS and consults GOTO; accept recognizes completion; error reports an invalid situation. For A→XYZ, pop three grammar symbols and their states, expose state q, then push A and GOTO[q,A]. “Go” is not a separate standard shift-reduce ACTION, although GOTO is essential table machinery.

questions.stem: In the context of code generation, what is a 'basic block'?

options.label: A
options.text: A block of memory allocated on the heap |

options.label: B
options.text: A maximal straight-line sequence of instructions with one entry point and one exit point

options.label: C
options.text: A function or procedure in the source code |

options.label: D
options.text: A group of related variable declarations

questions.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.

answer.text: A maximal straight-line sequence with entry at the beginning and exit at the end.
answer.explanation: COMP28 directly defines this sequence as a basic block. Maximality means it is not arbitrarily shortened while retaining the same entry/exit structure. Heap allocation, whole functions and related declarations describe different entities; a function may contain many basic blocks separated by branch targets and control transfers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A heap memory region is storage, not a straight-line control-flow unit.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This matches the maximal straight-line single-entry, end-exit definition in COMP28.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A function may contain branches and multiple basic blocks rather than one straight-line block.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Related declarations are not the instruction sequence defined by control-flow boundaries.

evidence.quote: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence entered at its beginning and exited at its end. Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and each instruction after a branch. Start a block at each leader and continue until the next leader.

A control-flow graph has blocks as vertices and possible next-block transfers as edges, including fall-through. A node D dominates N when every entry-to-N path passes through D. For an edge N→H where H dominates N, H is a loop header of a natural loop. This structure supports loop analysis. An expression DAG records value dependencies, not arbitrary control flow.

questions.stem: What is 'alias analysis' and why is it important for optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Determining which variables have the same name in different scopes; important for scope resolution |

options.label: B
options.text: Determining whether two pointer expressions can refer to the same memory location; important because aliasing restricts reordering and CSE

options.label: C
options.text: Detecting variables with the same type; important for type coercion |

options.label: D
options.text: Finding duplicate function names; important for linking

questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.text: Determine whether references may denote the same memory, constraining transformations.
answer.explanation: COMP33 asks whether references can designate the same memory. A write through p can invalidate a value loaded through q unless nonaliasing or another proof permits reuse. Therefore alias facts constrain CSE and reordering. Identical spellings, types or function names concern scope, typing or linkage rather than memory-location overlap.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Equal spelling in different scopes concerns declaration identity rather than whether references share memory.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Potential shared locations determine whether writes can invalidate reused loads or reordered memory operations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Equal types do not prove shared addresses and are not the alias-analysis question.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Duplicate linker names concern symbol resolution rather than potential overlap of referenced memory.

evidence.quote: Optimization preserves defined observable behavior, including required side effects and exceptions. Alias analysis asks whether references can denote the same memory. After *p=5, a previous load through q cannot be reused unless p and q are known not to alias or an equivalent proof applies. Function calls can also invalidate memory facts.

Do not move a potentially trapping division outside a loop that might execute zero times. Floating-point reassociation can change rounding and NaN behavior. Signed C/C++ overflow and shift rules differ from unsigned modular arithmetic; a mathematical identity is not automatically a legal transformation. Dependence analysis must show that fusion or scheduling preserves the required order of memory accesses.

questions.stem: Which statement about recursive-descent parsers is TRUE?

options.label: A
options.text: They cannot handle left-recursive grammars without modification |

options.label: B
options.text: They inherently support all context-free grammars

options.label: C
options.text: They require a parsing table to function |

options.label: D
options.text: They build the parse tree bottom-up

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Ordinary recursive descent needs modification to handle left recursion.
answer.explanation: COMP12 explains that ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever on left recursion before consuming a token. Removing left recursion or changing the algorithm is therefore necessary for that direct implementation. Recursive descent is top-down and normally procedural, so it does not inherently require an explicit table or support every CFG unchanged.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Without transformation or algorithmic modification, left recursion can cause infinite recursive calls before input consumption.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Ordinary recursive descent is not an unrestricted parser for every context-free grammar.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Procedures can encode production choices directly; an explicit parsing table is not required.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Recursive descent expands productions top-down rather than constructing a reverse-rightmost bottom-up parse.

evidence.quote:
Immediate left recursion has A→Aα. For A→Aα|β, where β does not start with A, introduce a new nonterminal A′ and use:
A→βA′
A′→αA′|ε
This preserves the generated language; tree shape changes, so semantic actions must preserve intended associativity. Indirect left recursion follows a cycle through other nonterminals and also needs removal for ordinary predictive descent.

Left factoring rewrites A→αβ|αγ using:
A→αA′
A′→β|γ
It postpones a choice until after the common prefix. It does not by itself remove ambiguity or guarantee LL(1). LR parsers can handle suitable left-recursive grammars; ordinary unmodified recursive descent can recurse forever before consuming input.

questions.stem: In attribute grammar terminology, which of the following is an 'inherited' attribute?

options.label: A
options.text: The value of an expression node computed from its children |

options.label: B
options.text: The type environment passed from a function declaration down to its body

options.label: C
options.text: The size of an array determined from its element type and length |

options.label: D
options.text: The result type of an arithmetic operation

questions.hint: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information.

answer.text: A type environment passed from a declaration into its body is inherited.
answer.explanation: COMP24 explicitly gives the declaration’s type environment passed into its body as an inherited attribute. This carries context inward rather than computing a parent from child values. Expression values, array sizes computed from components and arithmetic result types are ordinarily synthesized examples when obtained from the node’s own child information.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Computing an expression from its children is synthesized upward flow.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The surrounding declaration supplies type context to the nested body, matching the explicit inherited example.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Computing size from element information and length is a synthesized result, not supplied surrounding context.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An operation’s result type derived from operands is normally synthesized from its child information.

evidence.quote: A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions. An annotated parse tree displays computed attribute values; it is not itself an inherited or synthesized attribute. Synthesized attributes flow from children to a parent; inherited attributes carry context from parent or siblings.

For E→E1+T, E.val=E1.val+T.val synthesizes an expression value. A declaration’s type environment passed into its body is inherited. S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit LR reduction-time evaluation naturally; suitable LL parsers can also compute them. L-attributed definitions restrict dependencies so a left-to-right traversal can evaluate inherited context. Attribute dependency cycles can prevent evaluation.

questions.stem: A compiler emits the error 'variable used before initialization'. This is detected during:
questions.hint: Track which facts can hold along one path and which must hold along every path. Apply the specified direction, transfer rule and join operation.

answer.explanation: COMP29 distinguishes definite assignment, which asks whether initialization occurs on every incoming path, from reaching definitions alone. Such control/data-flow facts go beyond recognizing legal tokens or grammar. The error therefore belongs to semantic/data-flow analysis before target emission, even though exact acceptance and diagnostic rules depend on the language.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Scanning recognizes identifier tokens but does not prove initialization along every control-flow path.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A grammatically valid variable use can still occur before initialization.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Semantic data-flow analysis checks that required initialization precedes each use on every relevant path.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Target generation ordinarily consumes checked input rather than supplying the primary definite-assignment analysis.
