evidence.quote: Liveness is backward may-analysis: a value might be read before redefinition on some future path. OUT[B]=union of IN over successors; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]). Iterate to a fixed point. Liveness supports register allocation and dead-value removal. Definite-assignment analysis asks whether initialization occurs on every path before use; reaching definitions alone does not prove this.

questions.stem: In graph-coloring register allocation, what is an 'interference graph'?

options.label: A
options.text: A graph where nodes represent machine instructions and edges represent data dependencies |

options.label: B
options.text: A graph where nodes represent variables and edges connect pairs of variables that are simultaneously live

options.label: C
options.text: A graph where nodes represent registers and edges represent compatibility |

options.label: D
options.text: A graph representing the control flow of the program

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: A graph connecting values that must coexist in distinct registers.
answer.explanation: COMP36 models concurrently needed values as vertices joined by interference edges, with physical registers represented by colors. Thus the variable/live-range graph in B is the intended model. Instruction dependencies and control-flow edges have different meanings; a graph of register compatibility reverses the allocation model’s vertices and does not express live-value interference.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Instruction-dependency edges constrain scheduling rather than describing interference among live values.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Variables or live ranges form vertices; an edge requires distinct registers for simultaneously needed values.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Registers are colors in this model, not the vertices whose live ranges interfere.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A CFG connects basic blocks by possible transfers, not values by register interference.

evidence.quote: A value is live where it can be used before redefinition. In the interference model, values that must coexist in distinct registers are connected by an edge; each register is a color. Nonoverlapping live ranges may share a register. If a valid assignment cannot fit the available registers, spilling places selected values in memory and inserts loads/stores.

The general graph k-colorability decision problem is NP-complete for fixed k≥3; optimal register assignment/spill minimization is a hard optimization problem in general, so practical allocators use heuristics.

questions.stem: What is 'dead code' in the context of compiler optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Code that causes a runtime error |

options.label: C
options.text: Code that is unreachable or whose computed results are never used |

options.label: D
options.text: Code that depends on uninitialized variables

questions.hint: Trace whether computation is evaluated, moved, shared or removed. Preserve observable effects and use the stated arithmetic and target assumptions.

answer.text: Unreachable code or unused computations without required effects.
answer.explanation: COMP30 permits removing unreachable code and unused computations only when evaluation has no necessary side effects. C states the intended two dead-code categories, with this semantic caveat. Runtime faults, syntax defects and uninitialized uses are different error categories, not definitions of code being safely removable. An unused volatile read or effectful call may still be required.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A runtime fault does not make arbitrary reachable code safely removable as dead code.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Syntactically invalid code is a compilation error, not the definition of dead computation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unreachability or unused results identify candidates, provided necessary observable side effects are preserved.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: An uninitialized dependency is an analysis or correctness issue, not automatically dead code.

evidence.quote: Constant folding evaluates constant expressions during compilation: 3*4→12. Constant propagation substitutes known values: x=3; y=x+2 becomes y=3+2 before folding. Copy propagation substitutes a copied name while its source remains unchanged. Dead-code elimination removes unreachable code or computations whose values are unused and whose evaluation has no necessary side effects.

questions.stem: What is the precise relationship between the general term compiler and the term transpiler?

options.label: A
options.text: A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler; compilers can also target assembly, machine code or bytecode.

options.label: B
options.text: A compiler is faster than a transpiler

options.label: C
options.text: A transpiler performs more optimizations than a compiler |

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler; compilers can also target assembly, machine code or bytecode.
answer.explanation: A compiler translates a source program to an equivalent target representation, which may be machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language. A transpiler is the source-to-source subtype of compiler. This gives a meaningful target-based distinction while retaining the shared category. Speed and optimization count depend on implementations and workloads; neither defines the relationship between the two terms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A transpiler is a compiler whose target is another source language.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: There is no universal speed ordering.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Optimization count does not define the subtype.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The source-to-source target is a meaningful distinction.

evidence.quote: A compiler translates a source program into an equivalent target representation while preserving defined observable behavior. The target may be machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language. A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler, not a fundamentally separate noncompiler technology. A compiler preserves language semantics, not the programmer’s unstated intention.

An interpreter executes a program representation; it need not work one source line at a time. Systems can compile to bytecode and then interpret or JIT-compile it. AOT compilation happens before execution; JIT compilation happens during execution and may use runtime profiles. Neither is universally faster; startup cost, optimization and workload matter.

questions.stem: In the context of lexical analysis, 'lexeme' vs 'token' means:

options.label: A
options.text: Lexeme is the abstract category; token is the actual text |

options.label: B
options.text: Lexeme is the actual sequence of characters in the source; token is the abstract category with optional attribute value

options.label: D
options.text: Lexeme refers to keywords only; token refers to all other units

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Lexeme is the source text; token is its category with optional attributes.
answer.explanation: COMP04 directly distinguishes the actual character sequence from its token category and optional attribute. For example, total is a lexeme that may produce an ID token associated with a symbol entry. Neither term is restricted to keywords; the same distinction applies to identifiers, numeric literals, operators and other lexical units.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This reverses the roles: the lexeme is concrete text and the token identifies its class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The concrete source sequence is the lexeme; category and optional information form the token.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The note explicitly separates the two abstractions rather than treating them as synonyms.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Lexemes include identifiers, literals and operators, not just keywords.

evidence.quote: A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42). A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42. A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class. The scanner emits an ordered token stream, not an unordered mathematical set.

Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes. Whitespace and comments are usually skipped while line/column positions are retained. In indentation-sensitive or newline-sensitive languages, layout can carry tokens. Parse-tree construction is a parser task; scanning can intern identifier spellings, but declaration scope and types need later analysis.

questions.stem: Under the general interference-graph model with fixed k≥3, which task is an NP-complete decision problem?

options.label: A
options.text: Converting an NFA to a DFA |

options.label: C
options.text: Deciding whether an arbitrary interference graph can use k registers without spilling, for fixed k≥3

options.label: D
options.text: Computing FIRST sets for a CFG

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: Deciding whether an arbitrary interference graph can use k registers without spilling, for fixed k≥3
answer.explanation: In the general interference model, simultaneously needed values are adjacent and registers are colors. Deciding whether the graph can be colored with k registers without spilling is general graph k-colorability, NP-complete for fixed k≥3. Optimal allocation is instead an optimization task. The other alternatives are construction or fixed-point tasks and do not state this membership-plus-hardness decision problem.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: NFA determinization is a construction task, even when its output is exponential.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: LL(1) table construction is not the specified graph-coloring decision task.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No-spill allocation is k-colorability under the stipulated general model.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: FIRST-set computation is a fixed-point task rather than this NP-complete decision form.

evidence.quote: A value is live where it can be used before redefinition. In the interference model, values that must coexist in distinct registers are connected by an edge; each register is a color. Nonoverlapping live ranges may share a register. If a valid assignment cannot fit the available registers, spilling places selected values in memory and inserts loads/stores.

The general graph k-colorability decision problem is NP-complete for fixed k≥3; optimal register assignment/spill minimization is a hard optimization problem in general, so practical allocators use heuristics.

questions.stem: What is the 'reaching definitions' data flow problem used for?

options.label: A
options.text: Determining which variables are live at each program point |

options.label: B
options.text: Determining which variable assignments might reach a given program point without being overwritten

options.label: C
options.text: Determining which expressions are available at each program point |

options.label: D
options.text: Determining which functions can be called from a given call site

questions.hint: Track which facts can hold along one path and which must hold along every path. Apply the specified direction, transfer rule and join operation.

answer.text: Assignments that may reach a point without being overwritten.
answer.explanation: COMP29 directly defines reaching definitions as assignments that can arrive at a point without a replacement definition on the path. Its join is union because one possible path suffices. Liveness asks about future uses, available expressions asks about previous computations on every path, and possible call targets is a separate analysis question.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Future reads before redefinition are the liveness question, not reaching definitions.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This is the exact assignment-and-no-overwrite property defined for reaching definitions.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Available expressions concerns prior computations with unchanged operands, not assignment definitions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Possible function targets concern call-graph or points-to analysis rather than reaching assignment definitions.

evidence.quote: Reaching definitions is forward may-analysis: which assignments can reach this point without a replacement definition? OUT=GEN∪(IN−KILL), with IN the union of predecessor OUT sets. Available expressions is usually forward must-analysis: an expression has been computed on every relevant path and its operands have not changed. Join with intersection.

questions.stem: In predictive (LL(1)) parsing, when should the parser use an ε-production A → ε?

options.label: A
options.text: When the lookahead token is in FIRST(A) |

options.label: B
options.text: When the lookahead token is in FOLLOW(A) and no other production for A begins with that token

options.label: D
options.text: Whenever the next token is not a keyword

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Use ε on an appropriate FOLLOW(A) lookahead with no competing alternative.
answer.explanation: COMP14 enters a nullable alternative under the left-hand nonterminal’s FOLLOW symbols and requires no conflicting production in that cell. An epsilon reduction consumes no input. FIRST(A) alone can refer to a nonempty alternative, while stack emptiness and token being a keyword do not define nullable-alternative selection. Thus B supplies the correct lookahead rule.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A FIRST terminal may require a nonempty alternative; FIRST(A) alone does not select epsilon.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: FOLLOW lookahead selects the nullable alternative when its predictive table cell has no competing production.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: An empty stack is not the rule for selecting a production for a pending nonterminal.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Keyword status has no general relation to a nonterminal’s nullable-production table entries.

evidence.quote: For every A→α, put it in M[A,a] for each terminal a in FIRST(α). If α is nullable, also enter it under every symbol in FOLLOW(A). More than one production in a cell is a conflict. Pairwise SELECT sets must be disjoint; SELECT(α)=FIRST(α)−{ε}, plus FOLLOW(A) when α is nullable. This also detects two nullable alternatives.

Initialize stack with $S. Match and pop terminals; for a nonterminal consult its row and lookahead, then push the chosen RHS in reverse. An ε production consumes no input. Accept when stack and input reach $. For A→a|ε with b∈FOLLOW(A), choose a on lookahead a and ε on b.

questions.stem: Which of the following correctly describes a 'dominator' in a control flow graph?

options.label: A
options.text: A node that is executed before all other nodes unconditionally |

options.label: B
options.text: Node D dominates node N if every path from the entry node to N must pass through D

options.label: C
options.text: The node with the most outgoing edges |

options.label: D
options.text: The unique successor of every conditional branch

questions.hint: Identify what the representation stores, what it omits and which later transformations it must support; separate a representation property from an algorithmic task.

answer.text: Every entry-to-N path passes through D.
answer.explanation: COMP28 defines domination relative to a particular node N: every path from entry to N must pass D. This is not a claim that D precedes every node in the program, nor is domination measured by out-degree or being a unique successor. The definition concerns unavoidable traversal on paths reaching the specified node.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A dominator is defined relative to a node, not necessarily as preceding all program nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This exactly states the all-entry-to-N-paths definition in COMP28.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The number of outgoing edges does not establish unavoidable traversal on paths.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Branch successor uniqueness is unrelated to the general dominator definition.

evidence.quote: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence entered at its beginning and exited at its end. Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and each instruction after a branch. Start a block at each leader and continue until the next leader.

A control-flow graph has blocks as vertices and possible next-block transfers as edges, including fall-through. A node D dominates N when every entry-to-N path passes through D. For an edge N→H where H dominates N, H is a loop header of a natural loop. This structure supports loop analysis. An expression DAG records value dependencies, not arbitrary control flow.

questions.stem: In SLR(1) parsing, the reduce action for production A → α is triggered when the lookahead is in:
questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: FOLLOW(A), once the item for A→α is complete.
answer.explanation: COMP17 says SLR uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. The completed item establishes that the right side has been recognized; FOLLOW restricts which lookaheads permit reducing it. FIRST information predicts beginnings instead, and FOLLOW of an arbitrary right-hand string is not the table rule used here.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: FIRST(A) concerns beginnings of derived strings rather than lookaheads after a completed A.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: SLR places a completed A-production reduction under the lookaheads in FOLLOW(A).

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: FIRST of the right side predicts starting tokens, not permitted post-recognition reduction lookaheads.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: SLR uses FOLLOW of the left-hand nonterminal A, not this right-side expression.

evidence.quote: SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items. LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts. The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.

A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous. Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG. Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.

questions.stem: What is 'escape analysis' and how does it help optimization?

options.label: A
options.text: Analysis to detect out-of-bounds array accesses; helps prevent security vulnerabilities |

options.label: B
options.text: Analysis to determine whether an object's reference can 'escape' the function where it is created; enables stack allocation of non-escaping objects

options.label: C
options.text: Analysis to find unreachable exception handlers; enables dead code elimination |

options.label: D
options.text: Analysis to track pointer arithmetic; enables bounds checking elimination

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: Determine whether references outlive or escape a region, enabling safe allocation changes.
answer.explanation: COMP37 asks whether an object/reference can outlive or be accessed outside its allocating region. A proven nonescaping object may use stack storage or be eliminated when lifetime and identity are preserved. Bounds checking, exception reachability and pointer arithmetic are separate analyses and do not define the reference-escape property described.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Array bounds concern index validity rather than whether references leave their allocation region.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Reference escape information can justify stack allocation when lifetime and identity remain correct.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unreachable exception handlers concern control-flow reachability, not reference lifetime or external access.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Pointer arithmetic tracking does not by itself define escape beyond a function or allocation region.

evidence.quote: Static storage lasts throughout execution; stack frames support nested calls and recursion; heap storage supports lifetimes beyond a call. A frame may contain parameters, return address, saved registers, locals and temporaries. Sizes, alignment and offsets are target-dependent; a two-byte int is an example, not a C++ guarantee.

A calling convention specifies argument and result locations, caller/callee-saved registers, stack alignment and frame responsibilities. Escape analysis asks whether an object/reference can outlive or be accessed outside a region such as its allocating call. Proven nonescaping allocations may use stack storage or be eliminated by scalar replacement, provided identity and lifetime semantics remain correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a valid reason why LALR(1) parsers may have reduce/reduce conflicts that canonical LR(1) parsers do not?

options.label: A
options.text: LALR(1) uses a larger parsing table than canonical LR(1) |

options.label: B
options.text: LALR(1) merges LR(1) states with the same core but different lookaheads, potentially merging incompatible lookahead sets

options.label: C
options.text: LALR(1) does not support left-recursive grammars |

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Merging equal-core LR(1) states can combine incompatible reduction lookaheads.
answer.explanation: COMP17 directly explains that LALR merges canonical states with identical LR(0) cores while unioning their lookahead sets. Distinctions that prevented competing reductions in separate states can disappear, creating reduce/reduce conflicts. This is not due to incorrect FOLLOW computation or rejection of left recursion; the loss comes from deliberate state merging.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Merging aims to reduce state count, and a larger table is not the reason for new conflicts.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Combining lookaheads of equal-core states can make previously separated reductions compete.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: LALR can handle suitable left-recursive grammars, as other LR methods can.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The conflict can arise from correct merging, without any erroneous FOLLOW-set computation.

evidence.quote: SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production. Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items. LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts. The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.

A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions. An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous. Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG. Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.

questions.stem: Which is a common implementation mechanism for runtime virtual dispatch in an object-oriented language, when the receiver’s class cannot be resolved statically?

options.label: A
options.text: Static binding of function calls at compile time |

options.label: B
options.text: A virtual method table (vtable) per class, with function pointers resolved at runtime

options.label: C
options.text: Inline expansion of all polymorphic calls |

options.label: D
options.text: Name mangling to distinguish overloaded functions

questions.hint: Match stored information to its lifetime, access path and calling-convention role; distinguish compile-time organization from run-time storage.

answer.text: A virtual method table (vtable) per class, with function pointers resolved at runtime
answer.explanation: A common implementation stores virtual-method entries in a per-class vtable and lets an object refer to the appropriate table. A virtual call selects the entry using the receiver’s runtime class. Static binding alone does not provide that selection for an unknown class. Mandatory inlining is not generally possible, and name mangling distinguishes linker symbols rather than selecting overrides at runtime.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Static binding alone does not choose by an unknown runtime class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A per-class vtable is the common mechanism described in the note.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Unknown runtime receivers prevent mandatory inlining of all polymorphic calls.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Name mangling identifies symbols rather than selecting overrides.

evidence.quote: Inlining replaces a call with a suitably renamed copy of its body, preserving argument evaluation, returns and side effects. It can remove call overhead and expose optimization opportunities, but may increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. A recursive function cannot simply be expanded without limit.

Virtual dispatch chooses an overridden method based on a receiver’s runtime class. A common implementation uses a per-class virtual-method table and an object pointer to the table; the call loads the selected entry. This is an implementation strategy, not a universal language requirement. Name mangling distinguishes linker symbols, often for overloads; it is not itself runtime method selection. Proven receiver types may permit devirtualization.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true about a 'well-formed' grammar for LL(1) parsing?

options.label: B
options.text: For every non-terminal A with productions A → α1 | α2 | ... | αn, no two alternatives share a common token in their FIRST sets, and if any αi derives ε, then FIRST(αj) and FOLLOW(A) are disjoint for all j ≠ i

options.label: D
options.text: It must have at least one ε-production

questions.hint: Use construction direction, lookahead and grammar restrictions. Distinguish algorithm families, implementations and coverage before comparing them.

answer.text: Disjoint predictive selections, including nullable FIRST/FOLLOW constraints.
answer.explanation: COMP14 requires that alternatives for a nonterminal select disjoint lookahead sets. B gives the standard FIRST separation and nullable-alternative FOLLOW restriction; shared epsilon alternatives would also violate pairwise FIRST disjointness. Left recursion and useful ambiguity are not acceptable LL(1) properties, and epsilon productions are optional rather than required.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary LL(1) grammars cannot retain left recursion that recurs without input consumption.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Disjoint alternative selections prevent multiple productions from occupying the same predictive table cell.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A useful ambiguous grammar cannot give a unique deterministic LL(1) parse.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A grammar may be LL(1) without any epsilon production.

evidence.quote: For every A→α, put it in M[A,a] for each terminal a in FIRST(α). If α is nullable, also enter it under every symbol in FOLLOW(A). More than one production in a cell is a conflict. Pairwise SELECT sets must be disjoint; SELECT(α)=FIRST(α)−{ε}, plus FOLLOW(A) when α is nullable. This also detects two nullable alternatives.

Initialize stack with $S. Match and pop terminals; for a nonterminal consult its row and lookahead, then push the chosen RHS in reverse. An ε production consumes no input. Accept when stack and input reach $. For A→a|ε with b∈FOLLOW(A), choose a on lookahead a and ε on b.

questions.stem: The primary difference between a 'compiler' and a 'just-in-time (JIT) compiler' is:

options.label: A
options.text: A JIT compiler produces faster code than an ahead-of-time compiler always |

options.label: B
options.text: A JIT compiler compiles code at runtime (during program execution), allowing it to use runtime profiling information for optimization, while an AOT compiler compiles before execution

options.label: C
options.text: A JIT compiler does not perform any optimization |

options.label: D
options.text: A JIT compiler only works for interpreted languages

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: JIT compiles during execution; AOT compiles before execution.
answer.explanation: COMP01 defines AOT before execution and JIT during execution, possibly using runtime profiles. Both are compilation, so the heading compiler versus JIT is better understood as AOT versus JIT. The timing contrast in B is correct, while no universal speed guarantee, absence of optimization or restriction to interpreted languages follows.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Neither AOT nor JIT is universally faster; startup and workload affect the comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Runtime compilation can use execution profiles, whereas AOT performs compilation before the run.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: JIT may optimize using runtime information rather than performing no optimization.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: JIT is an execution-time compilation strategy, not a technique restricted to a separately defined interpreted-language category.

evidence.quote: A compiler translates a source program into an equivalent target representation while preserving defined observable behavior. The target may be machine code, assembly, bytecode or another source language. A transpiler is a source-to-source compiler, not a fundamentally separate noncompiler technology. A compiler preserves language semantics, not the programmer’s unstated intention.

An interpreter executes a program representation; it need not work one source line at a time. Systems can compile to bytecode and then interpret or JIT-compile it. AOT compilation happens before execution; JIT compilation happens during execution and may use runtime profiles. Neither is universally faster; startup cost, optimization and workload matter.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of syntax-directed translation in a compiler?

options.label: A
options.text:
To interleave semantic analysis with syntax analysis using attributes attached to 
grammar symbols

options.label: B
options.text: To generate optimized machine code directly

options.label: D
options.text: To replace the parser with a finite automaton

questions.hint: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information.

answer.text: Associate semantic computations with grammatical structure and attributes.
answer.explanation: COMP24 attaches attributes and semantic rules to grammar symbols and productions; COMP25 executes translation actions during processing. This permits semantic work to follow parsing structure, as A states. It does not inherently bypass IR to optimized machine code, reduce to tokenization, or replace the parser with a finite automaton.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Attributes and rules connect grammatical structure to semantic computations during translation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Direct optimized machine-code production is not the required or exclusive purpose of syntax-directed translation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Tokenization is lexical analysis rather than grammar-directed semantic computation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Finite automata recognize ordinary token patterns and do not replace general nested-syntax parsing.

evidence.quote: A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions.

A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler. Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.

questions.stem: Straight directed translation uses:
questions.hint: Track where each computed value comes from and when each production action runs. Distinguish the representation from its attached information.

answer.text: Grammar with semantic rules, reading the misspelled term as syntax-directed translation.
answer.explanation: The stem’s Straight directed translation appears to be a damaged rendering of syntax-directed translation. Under that explicit reading, COMP24 defines a CFG with attributes and semantic rules, and COMP25 embeds translation actions in productions. D expresses that structure despite its spelling error. The other choices omit semantics or prescribe unrelated implementation details.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Pure lexical rules do not supply grammar-directed semantic attributes and computations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Backtracking is a parsing implementation choice, not the defining translation structure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A grammar without semantic attributes or rules does not describe the syntax-directed definition requested.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Reading sematic as semantic, this is the grammar-plus-semantic-rules structure of syntax-directed translation.

evidence.quote: A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions.

A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler. Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code. The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.

questions.stem: A compiler has produced checked three-address code for a function. Which description incorrectly places the ensuing target-lowering task within the standard compilation pipeline?

options.label: A
options.text: Code generation can be considered as the start phase of compilation

options.label: B
options.text: The target program is the output of the code generator

options.label: C
options.text: Checked intermediate code is supplied as input to the code generator.

options.label: D
options.text: It used to produce the target code for three-address statements.

questions.hint: Identify each activity’s input and output. Distinguish character recognition, grammatical structure, semantic checks and target implementation.

answer.text: Code generation can be considered as the start phase of compilation
answer.explanation: Code generation uses checked intermediate code to produce target instructions after the frontend has analyzed the source. It can lower each three-address operation into a suitable target sequence. Lexical analysis, not code generation, begins the standard pipeline. The input condition here means checked IR suitable for lowering; it is not a claim that all possible program bugs have been proved absent.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Target lowering follows scanning, parsing, semantic checks and IR construction; it does not start compilation.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The generator’s output is target code.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Checked IR is the stated input to target lowering.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Three-address statements can be translated into target instructions.

evidence.quote: The conventional sequence is lexical analysis → syntax analysis → semantic analysis → intermediate-code generation → optimization → target-code generation. Scanning turns characters into tokens; parsing builds structure; semantics checks declarations and types; synthesis produces implementation code. A phase is a logical activity; a pass is a traversal that can combine activities.
Code generation lowers checked IR to a target form.

A token is a category with optional attribute, such as (ID, symbol-entry) or (INT_LITERAL,42).
A lexeme is the actual character sequence, such as total or 42.
A pattern specifies which lexemes belong to a token class.
The scanner emits an ordered token stream, not an unordered mathematical set.
Keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuation are token classes.

Regular expressions use concatenation, alternation r|s, Kleene star r* for zero or more, and r+ for one or more.
In a simplified alphabet, identifier = Letter(Letter|Digit)*; it permits a single letter and forbids a leading digit.
A C-like ASCII rule commonly also allows underscore: [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]* State the convention instead of claiming this covers every language’s identifiers.
Letter(Letter+|Digit*)* denotes the same language as Letter(Letter|Digit)* under ordinary regular-expression semantics: repeated blocks can contain any trailing letter/digit sequence.
These two regular expressions are equivalent.
Regular patterns handle ordinary tokens; arbitrary balanced nesting generally needs grammar/stack structure.

blocks.text: A common generator pipeline is regular expressions → NFA using Thompson construction → DFA using subset construction; minimization is optional.
For concatenation rs, connect r’s final state to s’s start by ε.
Alternation introduces branching ε paths; star adds a way to skip and repeat the fragment.
The ε-closure of states includes those reachable by zero or more ε edges.
A DFA state is a set of NFA states; its a-transition is ε-closure(move(set,a)).
Start with the NFA start closure, repeatedly add unseen subsets, and mark subsets containing an NFA final state as accepting.
Token identity and rule priority annotate accepting states; the empty subset acts as a dead state.

At each input position, choose the longest matching lexeme; if equal lengths match multiple flex rules, choose the earliest rule.
Thus ifx is an identifier rather than if followed by x; <= and ++ are each one operator token.
An implementation may recognize an identifier first and then consult a keyword table.
The increment operator is one token.
A comment contributes no ordinary parser token after preprocessing.

A lexical error prevents forming a legal token, such as an invalid character or unterminated literal.
A syntax error is an illegal token arrangement, such as a missing delimiter.
A semantic error violates name, scope or type rules after grammatical recognition.
A wrong algorithm can compile successfully; compilers do not detect all logical mistakes.
In the malformed C line fro ((I = o, I;, fro and lowercase o are legal identifier lexemes.
Misspelling for does not turn fro into a lexical error; mismatched syntax is definite, and undeclared o can also produce a semantic diagnostic.
Recovery order and exact diagnostics depend on the compiler.
Do not silently replace o by 0 or fro by for.

A context-free grammar G=(N,T,P,S) has nonterminals N, terminals T, productions P and start S. A production A→α rewrites one nonterminal.
A sentential form is any string of terminals/nonterminals derivable from S; a sentence contains only terminals.
A leftmost derivation rewrites the leftmost remaining nonterminal; a rightmost one rewrites the rightmost.
A parse tree shows grammar productions: root S, internal nonterminals, and terminal leaves, with ε sometimes shown for empty productions.
Its left-to-right yield is the input.
An AST omits grammar scaffolding and punctuation; expression operands are leaves and operators internal nodes.
The parser can build either representation, depending on implementation.

A grammar is ambiguous if at least one terminal string has two different parse trees, equivalently two leftmost derivations.
Merely changing derivation order on the same tree does not establish ambiguity.
E→E+E|E*E|id allows different trees for id+id*id.

For subtraction, a−b−c then groups (a−b)−c. The dangling-else grammar permits else to attach to either nested if; a nearest-unmatched-if rule or grammar rewrite resolves it.
Taking a leftmost derivation by itself does not resolve ambiguous interpretation.

Top-down parsing starts with S and expands productions toward the input, usually constructing a leftmost derivation.
Recursive descent typically has one procedure per nonterminal.
A general recursive-descent implementation can backtrack; a predictive parser chooses a production using lookahead without backtracking.
LL(1) scans Left to right, produces a Leftmost derivation and uses one lookahead token.
A nonrecursive predictive parser stores grammar symbols on an explicit stack and consults a table.
It is another implementation of predictive parsing, not a wholly different language class.
Table-driven and recursive predictive implementations can both be linear for a fixed suitable grammar.
Efficiency cannot be ranked from their names alone.

Bottom-up parsing starts from input and reduces toward S, constructing a rightmost derivation in reverse.
A handle is a production RHS occurrence whose reduction is the next step of that reverse derivation.
Not every substring matching a RHS is a handle in the current context.
Shift pushes the next input token and a state; reduce replaces a recognized RHS by its LHS and consults GOTO; accept recognizes completion; error reports an invalid situation.
For A→XYZ, pop three grammar symbols and their states, expose state q, then push A and GOTO[q,A]. “Go” is not a separate standard shift-reduce ACTION, although GOTO is essential table machinery.
Compiler Design module
Augment the grammar with S′→S. An LR(0) item A→α·β records progress through a production.
CLOSURE(I) repeatedly adds B→·γ whenever an item has its dot before nonterminal B and B→γ is a production.
GOTO(I,X) moves the dot past X in every eligible item and takes closure.
Start with CLOSURE({S′→·S}); repeatedly compute nonempty GOTO sets for all grammar symbols until no new state appears.
The resulting set of item sets is the canonical collection, not GOTO itself.
One transition

items.text: For S→a, call the initial closure I0: I0 = {S′→·S, S→·a} GOTO(I0,a) = {S→a·} GOTO(I0,S) = {S′→S·} Each complete set above is one state, not one state per item.

blocks.text: Allan Gottlieb, NYU Compilers Lecture 7
SLR(1) uses LR(0) states and FOLLOW(A) for reduction by a completed A production.
Canonical LR(1) attaches context-specific lookahead to items.
LALR(1) merges canonical states with the same LR(0) core, combining lookaheads; merging can introduce reduce/reduce conflicts.
The standard grammar-class hierarchy is LR(0)⊆SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), with increasing capability and often table size.
A shift/reduce conflict offers both consuming a token and reducing; reduce/reduce offers two reductions.
An SLR or LALR conflict does not by itself prove the grammar ambiguous.
Canonical LR(1) handles LR(1) grammars, not every unambiguous CFG.
Precedence and associativity can resolve suitable expression conflicts; changing parser names alone does not repair all ambiguity.
Compiler Design module
GNU Bison manual
LL, LR and recursive-descent parsers can all handle nested parentheses for suitable grammars.
An explicit or implicit stack, not the LR label alone, supports unbounded nesting.
Both LL and LR can use parsing tables.
Deterministic LL/LR grammars must be unambiguous; a general ambiguous grammar requires rewriting, disambiguation policy or a generalized method such as GLR.
An operator grammar conventionally forbids adjacent nonterminals on a RHS and usually ε productions.
Operator-precedence parsing additionally requires conflict-free precedence relations.
Ordinary right-linear regular grammars also lack adjacent nonterminals, so that property alone does not uniquely identify the operator-grammar category.
Regular patterns are chiefly lexical specifications; CFGs chiefly describe nested syntax.
Compiler Design module
A symbol table maps names or symbol identities to attributes: type, scope, width, storage offset, parameter signature, constant information or linkage.
A hash table gives expected O(1) insertion/lookup with suitable hashing; a stack of scope tables supports lexical nesting.
Search the nearest scope first, insert declarations in the current scope, and remove visibility when leaving it.
Scanning may intern a spelling first; semantic analysis determines the declaration and type.
Implementations differ, so first interaction is conventional rather than universal.
Not every punctuation token needs a symbol-table entry; literals may use a separate literal table.
A hash table is an implementation, not the information’s semantic role.
Compiler Design module

notes.title: Names, types and advanced language features

blocks.text: Distinguish lexical recognition, grammatical structure and semantic constraints.
In obj.method(x), the scanner recognizes identifiers and punctuation; the parser recognizes a member call; semantic analysis resolves the receiver, accessible member and argument types.
Overload resolution chooses among signatures using static types; overriding can select an implementation at runtime.

Nested scopes require declaration identity rather than spelling alone: an inner int x can shadow an outer float x. Closures capture free variables from lexical environments; lifetime can outlive the creating stack frame.
Generic functions need parameter constraints or instantiation checks.
These features require symbol/type information beyond a CFG, even when their surface syntax is context-free.
Specify and check a member call

items.text: For object.resize(3), the token kinds are id, dot, id, left parenthesis, integer, right parenthesis. One small grammar is Call → Expr . id ( Args ); Expr → id; Args → Expr | integer | ε. Derive Call ⇒ Expr . id ( Args ) ⇒ id . id ( integer ), then bind the tokens object, resize and 3. The parser checks this shape. Name and type analysis then require object to be in scope, resize to be an accessible member and an overload accepting one integer-compatible argument. If only resize() exists, the text still parses but fails the argument/type check.

blocks.text: Compiler Design module
Static checks occur before execution: type compatibility, duplicate declarations within a restricted scope, valid names, argument counts, return compatibility and control-flow placement.
A break is valid only in constructs allowed by the language; in C/C++ it can exit a loop or switch.
A compiler may annotate an AST or create typed IR; there is no mandatory uniquely named output tree.
Dynamic checks depend on runtime values, such as some bounds and null checks.
Static analysis can prove some accesses safe or faulty; “all memory errors cannot be statically checked” is too strong.
Unreachable code is not universally a semantic error: some languages reject it in specified cases, others merely warn or optimize it away.
Compiler Design module
A type checker verifies that operations are defined for their operands.
In a simple strict language, integer mod requires two integers; array indexing requires an array and integer index; an if condition requires Boolean; assignment requires equal or convertible types.
Function calls check parameter count and compatibility, and returns match result types.
Type inference derives types from constraints: if x is integer and + expects numeric operands, infer the expression type from numeric promotion rules.
It is a static technique even without explicit annotations.

Operator overloading supplies multiple operation meanings, not a substitute for type checking. int x="hello" is a type mismatch in ordinary C++/Java; division by zero and bounds violations are not automatically operand-type mismatches.
Compiler Design module
Coercion is an implicit conversion permitted by the language; a cast requests an explicit conversion.
Widening often increases representable range, but can still lose precision: Java int→float is widening although large integers round.
Java int→long is exact.
Narrowing can lose range or fractional information.
In C++ ordinary int x=3.14 converts to 3 when representable; it is not inherently a type error. int x{3.14} is rejected as narrowing.
C++ floating-to-integer conversion discards the fraction and has undefined behavior if the truncated value is unrepresentable.
Java ordinary double→int assignment needs a permitted explicit cast.
Mixing char and int is ordinarily valid after promotion in C++/Java; do not import a fictitious universal ban.
C++ working draft, floating-integral conversions
Java Language Specification, conversions
A syntax-directed definition is a CFG with attributes on grammar symbols and semantic rules on productions.
An annotated parse tree displays computed attribute values; it is not itself an inherited or synthesized attribute.
Synthesized attributes flow from children to a parent; inherited attributes carry context from parent or siblings.
For E→E1+T, E.val=E1.val+T.val synthesizes an expression value.
A declaration’s type environment passed into its body is inherited.
S-attributed definitions use only synthesized attributes and fit LR reduction-time evaluation naturally; suitable LL parsers can also compute them.
L-attributed definitions restrict dependencies so a left-to-right traversal can evaluate inherited context.
Attribute dependency cycles can prevent evaluation.
Compiler Design module
A syntax-directed translation scheme embeds executable actions in productions; the actions run while translating a source program, not while generating the compiler.
Attributes may compute types, values, AST pointers or generated code.
The scheme defines an input-to-output translation, not merely an input language.
Create an identifier leaf with mkleaf(id,entry), a number with mkleaf(num,value), and an operator node with mknode(op,left,right).
For a−4+c, construct +(−(a,4),c).
Postorder traversal prints postfix: a 4 − c +.
A stack evaluator pushes operands and pops right then left operands for an operator.
Infix-to-postfix is useful for stack machines but not mandatory for all compilers.
Compiler Design module
IR separates source analysis from target implementation, allowing optimizers and backends to be reused.
It should be easy to generate, analyze, transform and lower.
Portability is an architectural benefit, not proof that every IR omits all target-dependent details.
ASTs, graphs, bytecode and TAC can all be IRs.
Ordinary TAC arithmetic has at most one operation, two sources and one destination: t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=t2.
Quadruples store (op,arg1,arg2,result); triples omit an explicit result field and refer to instruction positions.
Indirect triples reference a separate ordering list, easing rearrangement.
Trees describe expressions; DAGs share common subexpressions, while quadruples/triples are instruction-record structures.
Compiler Design module
A conditional expression can generate if a<b goto Ltrue; goto Lfalse; labels join control paths.
Short-circuit AND evaluates the right operand only after a true left operand; OR only after a false one.
Translating both eagerly can change side effects.
For a zero-based array with element width w and lower bound L, element i uses base+(i−L)*w, assuming fixed-width contiguous storage.
SSA gives each definition a distinct name.
At a join, x3=φ(x1 from B1,x2 from B2) chooses the incoming value according to the predecessor actually taken; it is not an arithmetic average.
SSA is a naming discipline over IR and commonly coexists with a control-flow graph.
Compiler Design module
LLVM Language Reference, phi instruction

notes.title: Basic blocks, flow graphs and dominators

blocks.text: A basic block is a maximal straight-line instruction sequence entered at its beginning and exited at its end.
Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and each instruction after a branch.
Start a block at each leader and continue until the next leader.
A control-flow graph has blocks as vertices and possible next-block transfers as edges, including fall-through.
A node D dominates N when every entry-to-N path passes through D. For an edge N→H where H dominates N, H is a loop header of a natural loop.
This structure supports loop analysis.
An expression DAG records value dependencies, not arbitrary control flow.
Compiler Design module
Reaching definitions is forward may-analysis: which assignments can reach this point without a replacement definition?
OUT=GEN∪(IN−KILL), with IN the union of predecessor OUT sets.
Available expressions is usually forward must-analysis: an expression has been computed on every relevant path and its operands have not changed.
Join with intersection.
Liveness is backward may-analysis: a value might be read before redefinition on some future path.
OUT[B]=union of IN over successors; IN[B]=USE[B]∪(OUT[B]−DEF[B]).
Iterate to a fixed point.
Liveness supports register allocation and dead-value removal.
Definite-assignment analysis asks whether initialization occurs on every path before use; reaching definitions alone does not prove this.
Compiler Design module
Constant folding evaluates constant expressions during compilation: 3*4→12.
Constant propagation substitutes known values: x=3; y=x+2 becomes y=3+2 before folding.
Copy propagation substitutes a copied name while its source remains unchanged.
Dead-code elimination removes unreachable code or computations whose values are unused and whose evaluation has no necessary side effects.
For const int x=8,y=16; if(x>y){int z=x+y;}, propagate the constants, fold 8>16 to false, then remove the unreachable branch.
Both compile-time evaluation and dead-code elimination apply.
Compare optimizations by their applicability and effect; several transformations may be appropriate.
Computing an unused volatile read or effectful call may still be required.
Compiler Design module
Common-subexpression elimination reuses an earlier value only if operand values and relevant memory remain unchanged.
A DAG can represent sharing.

Algebraic simplification removes identities when valid: integer x+0→x. Strength reduction replaces an operation with an equivalent cheaper form, such as unsigned x*8→x<<3 for a valid width and shift count.
Target costs determine whether it is actually cheaper.
Peephole optimization examines short instruction windows.

It can remove redundant loads/stores, replace machine idioms and shorten jump chains: jump L1 where L1 immediately jumps L2 can become jump L2. Local optimization is a wider category; peephole optimization is a concrete method within the relevant scope.
Compiler Design module
A loop-invariant expression has unchanged inputs during a loop.
Hoist it to a preheader only when evaluation is safe on the paths where it will newly run.
Induction variables change by a loop-invariant increment, such as i=i+1.
For repeated t=4*i, maintain a running t increased by 4 when equivalent, reducing repeated multiplication.
Loop fusion or jamming combines loops with compatible bounds and safe dependence order.
Unrolling replicates a body to reduce branch overhead and expose parallelism; handle remaining iterations and increased code size.
Loop-invariant code motion, fusion, unrolling and strength reduction are different transformations.
A finite taxonomy needs a criterion: machine dependent/independent versus local/global/loop are different classifications.
Compiler Design module
Optimization preserves defined observable behavior, including required side effects and exceptions.
Alias analysis asks whether references can denote the same memory.
After *p=5, a previous load through q cannot be reused unless p and q are known not to alias or an equivalent proof applies.
Function calls can also invalidate memory facts.
Do not move a potentially trapping division outside a loop that might execute zero times.
Floating-point reassociation can change rounding and NaN behavior.
Signed C/C++ overflow and shift rules differ from unsigned modular arithmetic; a mathematical identity is not automatically a legal transformation.
Dependence analysis must show that fusion or scheduling preserves the required order of memory accesses.
Compiler Design module
Code generation lowers checked IR to a target form.

Instruction selection chooses target operations; register allocation chooses where values reside; scheduling orders instructions while respecting dependencies; storage layout assigns offsets and follows ABI requirements.
Register assignment names actual physical registers after allocation decisions.
For t=a+b, a simple target could emit LOAD R1,a; LOAD R2,b; ADD R3,R1,R2; STORE t,R3.
Other targets may combine loads with arithmetic or keep t in a register.
Machine idioms, register availability and instruction order affect execution time.

Absolute machine code, relocatable object code, assembly and VM bytecode can be legitimate compiler targets; TAC is normally intermediate, but “cannot ever be target code” is an unjustified universal.
Compiler Design module
LLVM target-independent code generator
A register descriptor records which current values are held in a register.
An address descriptor for a name records all current locations containing its value, possibly memory and multiple registers.
A memory copy can become stale after a register-only assignment.
These are code-generator bookkeeping structures, not source-language types.
A simple code-generation algorithm calls getReg for a TAC instruction to select operand/result registers, emits necessary loads, emits the operation, then updates descriptors.
Prefer an already suitable register or a reusable dead operand; otherwise choose a spill victim and store any live value lacking another current copy.
At a block exit, preserve values needed by successors.
Allan Gottlieb, NYU Compilers Lecture 14
A value is live where it can be used before redefinition.
In the interference model, values that must coexist in distinct registers are connected by an edge; each register is a color.
Nonoverlapping live ranges may share a register.
If a valid assignment cannot fit the available registers, spilling places selected values in memory and inserts loads/stores.

The general graph k-colorability decision problem is NP-complete for fixed k≥3; optimal register assignment/spill minimization is a hard optimization problem in general, so practical allocators use heuristics.
Restricted interference graphs or SSA formulations can have different properties.
Do not describe every possible register-allocation algorithm as NP-complete merely because a general model is difficult.
Cornell CS4120, Register Allocation notes
Static storage lasts throughout execution; stack frames support nested calls and recursion; heap storage supports lifetimes beyond a call.
A frame may contain parameters, return address, saved registers, locals and temporaries.
Sizes, alignment and offsets are target-dependent; a two-byte int is an example, not a C++ guarantee.
A calling convention specifies argument and result locations, caller/callee-saved registers, stack alignment and frame responsibilities.
Escape analysis asks whether an object/reference can outlive or be accessed outside a region such as its allocating call.
Proven nonescaping allocations may use stack storage or be eliminated by scalar replacement, provided identity and lifetime semantics remain correct.
Compiler Design module
Inlining replaces a call with a suitably renamed copy of its body, preserving argument evaluation, returns and side effects.
It can remove call overhead and expose optimization opportunities, but may increase code size and instruction-cache pressure.
A recursive function cannot simply be expanded without limit.
Virtual dispatch chooses an overridden method based on a receiver’s runtime class.
A common implementation uses a per-class virtual-method table and an object pointer to the table; the call loads the selected entry.
This is an implementation strategy, not a universal language requirement.
Name mangling distinguishes linker symbols, often for overloads; it is not itself runtime method selection.
Proven receiver types may permit devirtualization.
Compiler Design module
Panic-mode recovery skips input until a synchronizing token such as ; or } permits parsing to resume.
Phrase-level recovery makes a local insertion/deletion.
Report the location and cause while avoiding cascades of misleading diagnostics.
Lexical, syntax and semantic phases each detect their own errors; error handling is a shared service.
Lex/flex generates scanners from patterns and actions.
Yacc means Yet Another Compiler Compiler; Yacc/Bison generates parsers from grammar rules and semantic actions.
Typical specification files have definitions, %% rules, and %% user code.
Classic Yacc uses LALR; Bison supports additional LR and generalized modes.
Scanner generation does not replace the CFG parser.
Compiler Design module

notes.title: Trace one expression through the compiler

blocks.text: For a=b+c*d;, the scanner recognizes names and operators, the parser forms an assignment with +(b,*(c,d)), and semantic analysis resolves declarations and operand/result types.
A declaration such as float a; int b,c,d; can require a conversion before storing the numeric result, according to language arithmetic rules.
Generate t1=c*d; t2=b+t1; a=convert_if_needed(t2).
Constant operands can fold; repeated unchanged expressions can share values.
Finally choose target instructions and registers.
The same spelling a can denote different declarations in nested scopes.
At each step ask what representation enters, what new information is added, and which errors can now be justified.
Compiler Design module

notes.title: Distinguish tokens, lexemes and lexical analysis

blocks.text: The primary output of lexical analysis is a token stream, rather than a symbol table, AST or assembly; some are side structures. Distinguish a token category from the lexeme text that matches it.
Counting the loop header gives 14 tokens, even if no option matches.
Grouping characters into token classes is lexical analysis; grouping tokens into expressions and statements is syntax analysis.
Identify whether an analysis groups characters into tokens or tokens into syntactic constructs.
Symbol tables store identifiers and their attributes, not obligatorily every kind of token.
Trees store hierarchical constructs, while a symbol table stores declaration metadata.
Compiler Design module

notes.title: Compare parser methods and grammar conditions

blocks.text: Shift-reduce and LR are both bottom-up rather than top-down methods.
Recursive and nonrecursive predictive parsers can both be efficient.
Nested parentheses and parsing tables do not uniquely identify LR.
Ambiguity does not disappear merely by choosing LR, and leftmost derivation is not an ambiguity-resolution policy.
Overlapping FIRST sets, left recursion and ambiguity can each prevent a useful grammar from being LL(1); do not restrict the check to only the first two.
Check all applicable conditions and identify any conflicting table cell.
Precedence versus operator-precedence parsing needs a concrete conflict and policy, not a blanket claim that every shift-reduce conflict has one solution.
Compiler Design module
Type checking and symbol tables are both important to semantic analysis: one is an activity and one a data structure.
Semantic rules generally compute attributes, including but not limited to types, values and code; no listed specialized purpose is automatically exhaustive.
Both names and types belong in symbol records.
Distinguish division by zero, bounds violations, indentation mistakes and syntax errors from type errors; a type-error example should specify the language and incompatible operands.
Code generation is conventionally last in a simplified pipeline even if later target optimization exists.
A compiler may emit an annotated AST or typed IR, so distinguish representation, annotation and phase before forcing one tree name.
Compiler Design module

notes.title: Parser direction, expression parsing and coverage

blocks.text: The common two-way classification of parsing is by construction direction: top-down parsing expands from the start symbol, while bottom-up parsing reduces the input toward that symbol. This counts broad directions, not the number of parser algorithms or implementations.

Operator-precedence parsing is a restricted bottom-up expression-parsing method using a stack and precedence relations. With a suitable expression grammar, the stack retains unfinished surrounding expressions while nested parentheses are processed.

In the standard comparison by grammar coverage, canonical LR(1) is more general than the restricted operator-precedence method. Together with SLR(1)⊆LALR(1)⊆LR(1), this makes canonical LR(1) the broadest of those named deterministic parsing methods. Broader coverage does not mean faster execution or smaller tables.

Compiler Design module · page 11

notes.title: Grammar notation and general CFG parsing algorithms

blocks.text: Backus–Naur form, or BNF, is a notation for context-free grammar production rules. It describes how syntactic constructs are formed; it is different from an abstract syntax tree representing one particular program.

CYK and Earley are context-free grammar parsing algorithms. They determine grammatical structure or membership of an input sequence. They are different tasks from Thompson construction, which builds a token-recognizing NFA from a regular expression, and subset construction, which turns an NFA into a DFA.
GNU Bison: Languages and Context-Free Grammars
Lark official documentation: parsing algorithms
Compiler Design module · page 8

notes.title: Equivalent specifications for ordinary token languages

blocks.text: Classical regular expressions, consistently right-linear regular grammars and finite automata describe the same regular-language family. Thus an ordinary token pattern specified by a regular expression also has a regular grammar and an equivalent finite-state recognizer.

This equivalence concerns expressive power, not spelling of the specification or implementation size. Context-free grammars can also describe regular languages, but their larger family is needed for syntax with unbounded nested structure rather than ordinary regular token patterns.
Automata and Complexity Theory module · page 7
Automata and Complexity Theory module · page 8

Instruction scheduling orders selected target instructions while preserving dependencies. A target-aware scheduler also considers instruction latencies and the processor resources needed by each operation. This is a backend optimization whose performance choices depend on the target machine, even when a reusable scheduling framework serves many targets.

By contrast, constant folding, dead-code elimination and safe loop-invariant motion can be expressed on a target-neutral IR using values, control flow and side-effect rules. Target costs can still influence whether a legal transformation is worthwhile. Machine independence therefore describes the abstraction of a pass, not freedom from all language semantics or implementation costs.
LLVM — The Target-Independent Code Generator
LLVM — TargetSchedModel reference

Allocate this course its official six-item priority. Compare scanner/parser/semantic checker and LL/LR, then trace concrete examples.
Practise token counting, FIRST/FOLLOW, predictive and LR actions, attribute flow, three-address code and safe optimization. State language and target assumptions.
Justify answers using compiler definitions, rules and traces. Check the scope and conditions of each claim using compiler theory.
